title: Insurance in Germany: what you need and what you can skip
description: Health, liability, household, accident, life and travel insurance in Germany, explained for newcomers with a note on which ones actually matter.
html:
Germans are famously well insured, and newcomers often feel pressure to buy policies they do not need. Some insurance is compulsory, some is strongly advisable and some is optional. Here is a practical ranking.

Health insurance: compulsory

Everyone living in Germany must be insured, either in the statutory or the private system. It is a condition of your visa and of university enrolment. Arrange it before you travel.

Personal liability: strongly advisable

Liability insurance (Haftpflicht) pays when you accidentally injure someone or damage their property, including your rented flat. German law makes you liable without limit, so a few euros a month buys protection against a potentially enormous bill. Almost every resident has it, and many landlords ask for it.

Household contents: advisable once you own things

Contents insurance (Hausrat) covers your belongings at home against fire, water, storm and burglary. For a student with a laptop and a bicycle it is optional; for a family with a furnished flat it is sensible. It is cheap and often bundled with liability cover.

Accident insurance: optional

Private accident insurance pays a lump sum for permanent disability after an accident. Employees are covered at work by the statutory scheme; the private version matters most for self-employed people and those with dangerous hobbies.

Life insurance: only with dependants

Term life insurance pays a sum to your family if you die. It is relevant if someone depends on your income, and irrelevant otherwise.

Repatriation cover: cheap peace of mind

Some policies cover the cost of transporting you home in a medical emergency or after death. Travel health insurance for newcomers often includes it.

Travel insurance

For the journey to Germany and the first weeks you need travel health insurance, which the visa requires. For later trips abroad, your German health insurance covers you in the EU; outside it, a cheap annual travel policy fills the gap.

In short

Health insurance is mandatory, liability is the one you should not skip, and everything else depends on your situation. Be sceptical of anyone trying to sell you a bundle in your first week.
